newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-NAGANO GAMES HAUNTED BY GHOSTS OF ATLANTA.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NAGANO GAMES HAUNTED BY GHOSTS OF ATLANTA.

text.p: The Ghosts of Atlanta are gathering over the 1998 Nagano Winter Games, threatening an unhappy farewell to the 20th century for the Olympic movement.

Organisers go into the one year countdown to the games on Friday with costs mounting, some sports federations and competitors unhappy, key logistics still unsolved, and even Japan's own Olympic chief warning of a "bad news" games.
Nagano Olympic Organising Committee (NAOC) director general Makoto Kobayashi believes the sour mood arises from his city having to pay the price for the mishaps of last year's Atlanta Olympics.
"We're getting a lot of extra demands from different organisations because there were so many mistakes at the Atlanta Olympics," he told Reuters.

NAOC officials say sports leaders came away from Atlanta determined to be firm in their demands for the best possible facilities and arrangements at the February 7-22 games, arguing the spectacle belongs to them, not the city that stages the event.

They feel pressed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to avoid the embarrassing transportation, computer and security problems that plagued the Atlanta Games, but seem not to have calculated in advance the investment that implies.
"We don't want to lose any buses, we don't want to lose any results, we don't want any security scares," one official said. "But that all costs money that we didn't count on."
Several sports have requested better technical arrangements and facilities for athletes and officials.

Skiing, the games highest-profile sport, wants a higher start for the mens downhill and floodlights for ski jumping. Ice hockey wants more seats. Figure skating wants better hotels. Alpine skiers want to lodge closer to their venues.

Media organisations are demanding cast-iron assurances there will be no repetition of the Atlanta results farce, when many competition results were either unavailable, riddled with errors, incomplete or simply incomprehensible.
"But we have other pressures on us as well," Kobayashi said. "A couple of years ago, no one had ski jumping nets. Now they're saying: we use them elsewhere, you should have them."
The NAOC is also under attack for their failure to supply enough Western-style hotel rooms and for reneging on a promise to foot the entire bill of transport expenses for athletes.
Tsuguto Kitano, head of the Nagano Prefectural Ski Federation, has called NAOC "largely a group of country bumpkins".
A Nagano official who requested anonymity told Japan's Kyodo News Service: "The problems just keep coming, one after another. I feel like I want to scream 'Hey, give us a break'."

Total operating expenses for the Games, the biggest ever with 68 events in 11 sports, have risen from an initial 76 billion yen ($800 million) to 94.5 billion yen ($995 million), with a final budget due at the end of March.
The costs have risen because, as the Japanese economy struggles out of recession, corporate handouts are not as generous as forecast when Nagano won the games in 1991.

"In the midst of the current severe economic situation all efforts are being made to secure revenues...," NAOC said in a statement last December. "Simple yet efficient games operations will be implemented to minimise expenditures."
The one bright spot for NAOC has been the strong dollar.

Kobayashi said the 95-yen-to-the-dollar exchange rate for the dollar-based price of television rights and international sponsorship contracts would be increased to reflect the yen's depreciation to its present level of about 120.
Trial competitions in Nagano and its venues have revealed other possible problems, with traffic snarled for hours around Hakuba after a World Cup ski jumping competition last month.
Fickle weather has also played havoc with preparations.

Heavy snow forced cancellation of a World Cup ski jumping event at Hakuba last month and two men's downhill races last year. In early January, a lack of snow caused nervous moments at a World Cup cross-country competition.
The woes last week led an exasperated Hironoshin Furuhashi, head of Japan's Olympic Committee and a NAOC vice-president, to say he had heard "nothing but bad news" about preparations.
"NAOC's way of doing things may or may not be bureaucratic, but it is one-sided," he told reporters. "If it continues like this, I think the Nagano Games will not be successful."
